newsitem.title: GERMANY: ProSieben shares calm after IPO storm.
newsitem.headline: ProSieben shares calm after IPO storm.

text.p: A week after their much-hyped launch following a frantic subscription period, shares in German television network ProSieben AG have settled at a solid but modest premium to their issue price.
The preference shares, issued last Monday at a price of 72 marks in a flotation which was 50 times oversubscribed, surged 32 percent on their bourse debut to close at 95 marks.

This Monday, ProSieben bucked a bullish trend to slide 55 pfennigs to 89.50 marks -- still 24 percent above their price at issue but nowhere near the lofty heights of up to 115 marks at which they traded in the "grey" market before their issue.
Analysts said the current price marked a sensible normalisation. Euphoria over the ProSieben share offer and a supply squeeze had inflated its price to an unrealistic degree.
"All the hot air is out now," said an analyst who did not wish to be named.
"When half of Germany has been chasing after one share, you are bound to lose grip of reality for a while. This (current level) is a good price," he added.

ProSieben is the first German television broadcaster to list its shares on the stock market. The company raised 1.26 billion marks ($709 million) through the issue, increasing its capital by 360 million marks to over 700 million marks.
ProSieben made liberal use of TV advertising to generate a public frenzy over its share offer which called to mind the massive and even glitzier Deutsche Telekom flotation last November.
Only one in 10 bidders eventually received any ProSieben shares at all, and even winners had only gained a portion of the shares they ordered.

"To those people lucky enough to get their hands on some of this stock, I would say hold on to them but I could not issue any kind of strong buy recommendation," said Petra Heist, analyst at Bayerische Vereinsbank AG.
"The share was priced well, but it wasn't cheap and I think this is a more normal level. We won't see much change in the short term," Heist added.
Analysts also noted that no major news was expected from ProSieben in the short term.
The company has released key figures for 1996, when its profits rose to 169 million marks from 96 million the year before while sales rose to 1.69 billion marks from 1.47 billion.

There are also some areas of uncertainty about ProSieben's future. Like the rest of Germany's closely-held media industry, the ProSieben offering is complicated and its future shareholding structure, the target of sharp criticism, has pros and cons for investors.
Ordinary shares in the company -- the only stock with voting rights -- are not yet listed.
Majority shareholder Thomas Kirch, with close ties to his father's film and television empire, holds 60 percent of the ordinary stock and retail group Rewe holds the other 40 percent.
Competitors have warned that Kirch could use his power to the detriment of private shareholders with stock but no say in the company. ProSieben has firmly denied that there is any such risk.
